description: We are a team passionate about technology and innovation, committed to developing solutions that help farmers face the challenges of climate change using NASA data, promoting more sustainable and resilient agriculture.
summary: RotaMaya is a web application that helps farmers in Yucatán decide what to plant, when to plant it, and how much to irrigate. It uses 41 years of Earth observation data from NASA. The peninsula's climate is changing: Oxkutzcab experiences almost six more days of extreme heat per decade, and in 2026, the rains arrived in Mérida 38 days late. Even so, most cornfields are planted according to the traditional calendar. RotaMaya transforms daily data from NASA POWER and soil moisture from SMAP into simple answers for each municipality: when the rains typically begin, how long the dry season lasts, which crops best withstand the local climate, and how many liters of water each crop needs based on soil type. A game-like simulator allows users to "plant" without risking the harvest and compare dates before making a decision. The tool supports the farmer's decision-making; it does not replace it.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works

The user enters their postal code, and the application displays the actual weather for their municipality:

when the rainy season typically begins and its range in 8 out of 10 years;

rainfall from May to October;

the number of days with temperatures exceeding 35°C (95°F);

the midsummer heat wave;

the water balance;

soil moisture, week by week.

Each data point shows its trend over 41 years and how the current season (2026) was. The weather for the last 30 days, taken from the daily NASA POWER API, is also displayed.

In the simulator, the user chooses one of 12 crops from the region (corn, beans, squash, habanero pepper, xpelón, henequen, jicama, melon, and others), the planting date, and the soil type:

k'ankab, deep red soil;

tzek'el, stony soil.

The plant grows week by week using the actual climate data from the last 41 years. Ultimately, the user sees three things:

the health of the crop;

the optimal planting date; and

the amount of water needed: liters per square meter, the frequency of watering, and the number of weeks during the growing season.

How it's calculated:

Daily climate data from NASA POWER for 1985 to 2026 is downloaded for each pilot municipality: Mérida, Tizimín, Valladolid, Tekax, and Oxkutzcab.

Using this data, metrics are calculated for each year: the start of the rainy season (using a rule that eliminates "false starts"), the midsummer drought, hot days, and water balance.

Evapotranspiration is obtained using the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method.

Each crop is cross-referenced week by week with the climate data for each year, using its crop coefficients (FAO-56) and the temperature that damages it (FAO ECOCROP and scientific literature). Irrigation depends on root depth, soil moisture (Table 19 of FAO-56), and the amount of soil between the rocks.

Expected Benefits and Impact

Fewer crops lost due to planting before the rainy season begins.

Better crop selection and rotations for each area.

More efficient water use, because irrigation recommendations are adapted to the soil type: the same corn requires 46 L/m² every 8 days in k'ankab soil and 6 L/m² daily in tzek'el soil.

Open scientific data presented in language any farmer can understand.

The approach can be replicated in any rainfed agricultural region worldwide.

Tools Used

Data: NASA POWER (daily API, AG community), NASA SMAP (SPL3SMP_E), SoilGrids, INEGI, FAO-56, and FAO ECOCROP. Processing: Python, with custom scripts for downloading, metrics, cross-cropping, trends, and format validation.

Web: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.

Collaboration and implementation: GitHub, GitHub Actions (automatic data and website validation), and Vercel.
